questions.q: In the toy dataset, k(A,B) for A at x=0.4 and B at x=0.5 is approximately 0.9975, a very high similarity. Why?
options: Because A and B have very close x-values (0.4 vs 0.5), and the angle-encoding kernel cos^2((x-x')/2) is near 1 for small differences
Because A and B have the same label, which directly determines the kernel value
Because the kernel formula always returns approximately 1 regardless of the input values
Because A and B were specifically chosen to be orthogonal in the encoding
questions.explain: The kernel depends purely on the difference in x-values via cos^2((x-x')/2) -- since 0.4 and 0.5 are close, cos(-0.05) is close to 1, squaring gives approximately 0.9975, independent of the labels.

questions.q: For the new test point D at x=0.45, the kernel values are k(D,A) ~ 0.9994, k(D,B) ~ 0.9994, and k(D,C) ~ 0.1342. What label does the kernel-weighted nearest-neighbor rule predict for D, and why?
options: Label 0, because D is far more similar to A and B (both label 0) than to C (label 1)
Label 1, because C has the highest kernel value
No prediction is possible since A and B tie exactly
Label 0 and label 1 simultaneously, since the kernel values are ambiguous
questions.explain: D's kernel similarity to A and B (both ~0.9994) is far higher than to C (~0.1342), so the nearest-neighbor-by-kernel rule predicts label 0, matching the intuition that x=0.45 sits right between A's 0.4 and B's 0.5.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say this toy lab does NOT demonstrate any advantage of the quantum kernel over a classical one?
options: A classical RBF kernel on the same three points with a comparable bandwidth would make the identical classification call, since the underlying 'D is between A and B' intuition doesn't require anything quantum
Because the quantum kernel actually produced the wrong classification in this example
Because quantum kernels cannot be computed for datasets smaller than 10 points
Because the lab used amplitude encoding, which is known to always underperform classical kernels
questions.explain: The classification outcome here follows purely from geometric closeness in the 1D feature space -- a classical kernel would reach the same conclusion, so this toy example illustrates mechanics only, not any quantum advantage, consistent with the course's honest framing.

questions.q: What four changes would turn this toy nearest-neighbor example into an actual trained SVM, per the lesson?
options: Many more training points, a full N x N kernel matrix, feeding that matrix to a classical SVM solver (e.g., SVC(kernel='precomputed')), and letting margin-maximization -- not a hand-picked nearest-neighbor rule -- determine the decision boundary
Switching to amplitude encoding, removing the kernel matrix entirely, and using basis encoding instead
Running the circuit on real NISQ hardware instead of a simulator, with no other changes
Replacing the kernel with a Euclidean distance metric, which is mathematically identical
questions.explain: A real implementation scales up the dataset, computes the full kernel matrix the same way, and hands it to a classical SVM solver whose margin-maximization optimization determines the actual decision boundary -- the nearest-neighbor rule here was only a hand-traceable simplification.

questions.q: For a new test point D at x=1.0, with A at x=0.4 and B at x=0.5, k(D,A) is approximately 0.9127 and k(D,B) is approximately 0.9388. Which training point is D more similar to, and does this match the raw distances |1.0-0.4|=0.6 and |1.0-0.5|=0.5?
options: D is more similar to B (higher kernel value), matching the fact that B is the closer point in raw feature distance (0.5 vs 0.6)
D is more similar to A, contradicting the raw distance intuition
D is equally similar to both A and B
The kernel values cannot be compared to raw distances in any way
questions.explain: k(D,B) > k(D,A) matches the raw distance ordering (B is 0.5 away, A is 0.6 away from D), confirming the angle-encoding kernel behaves consistently with simple distance intuition in this regime.
